newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany prepares for labour unrest over sick pay.
newsitem.headline: Germany prepares for labour unrest over sick pay.

text.p: Labour unrest reminiscent of the 1950s is brewing in Germany as Bonn steps up dismantling its famous social-welfare system credited with transforming the country's post-war rubble into an economic powerhouse.

A difficult autumn of industrial action appears to be ahead as unions threaten to strike over the implementation of Bonn's 70 billion marks ($46 billion) in spending cuts aimed at whipping Germany's finances into shape in 1997 for European currency union.

One aspect of the Bonn plan that has touched a raw nerve is the reduction in sick pay benefits. Many German corporations, led by industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG, this week jumped at the chance to enact the policy from next month.

The sick pay row, along with a new law giving employers more freedom to fire workers, are viewed as the last straw for unions, which have felt as though their backs were to the wall after being forced this year into compromise in wage talks and unaccustomed alliances with employers that have since soured.
And the tension does not help ahead of the start of wage negotiations for 1997 contracts, slated to begin in December.
German workers for years have enjoyed six weeks of full pay for sick leave, which comes in addition to the usual allotment of six weeks holiday.
The new law calls for sick time to be paid at 80 percent of normal salary, prompting protests which recall a 16-week strike in 1957 when employers sought to cut benefits.
Employer groups said they were seeking dialogue with unions over the issue, noting that German law forbids strikes over political issues.

Union actions will likely be tied to disputes over changing current contracts. The Bavarian unit of IG Metall, home to carmaker BMW AG and electronics group Siemens AG, said on Thursday it will cancel wage contracts in January to give it the option of launching strikes.
Germany's HBV retail, banking and insurance union on Thursday also threatened banks with strikes if they carried out plans to cut sick pay benefits under the new law.
"When a member of the family gets hit in the rear, others will not turn away," German Trade Union Federation tax expert Reinhard Dombre told the current edition of Spiegel magazine.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl has said he was forced to seek the urgent reform even if currency union were not an issue, saying the changes were needed to make Germany competitive in the rough-and-tumble world of international trade.

Top business leaders claim the strong mark and high labour costs are driving jobs abroad and keeping unemployment at home near post-war highs, which raises public spending and weighs on the deficit that needs to be cut for entry into currency union.

"If anything, if there was no currency union, the mark would be even more stronger and more efforts would be needed," said Alison Cottrell, international economist at PaineWebber in London. "Something clearly had to be done."
Sick pay has often been a nagging problem for companies, with the German engineering employers' association saying each worker took an average of two weeks sick time.
"The pressure has obviously intensified to change the system, which I think is clearly independent from the single European currency issue," said Holger Fahrinkrug, economist at UBS in Frankfurt.

"Bonn is taking advantage of the timing to pass new laws with unemployment so high," he said. "That makes it easier for the government to push it through because public opinion will be more accepting to fight joblessness."

Despite the unrest, few observers expect the sort of social unrest seen in France in the bid by Paris to cut social spending to meet deficit and debt criteria laid out in the Maastricht Treaty for entry into currency union in 1999. ($1=1.5206 Mark)
